results.name: late_minus_early_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate on trials with trial_index >= 300 minus yes-rate on trials with trial_index < 150; observed > model means people drift toward "yes" over the session more than the trial-invariant model predicts (observed < model means drift toward "no").

results.name: cell_consensus_all
results.description: Over all (set, target) cells with at least 5 responses, the mean of p*(1-p) where p is the cell's yes-rate; observed < model means people's answers to the same item are more consensual / all-or-none than the model's graded probabilities produce, observed > model means more within-item disagreement than predicted.

results.name: parity_mismatch_yes_rate
results.description: Among sets of 2+ examples that all share one parity, the yes-rate for targets of the opposite parity; observed > model means people use parity less strictly than the model predicts, observed < model means they reject parity violators more sharply than the model's rule/interval mixture with guessing allows.
results.code:
# name: parity_mismatch_yes_rate
# description: Among sets of 2+ examples that all share one parity, the yes-rate for targets of the opposite parity; observed > model means people use parity less strictly than the model predicts, observed < model means they reject parity violators more sharply than the model's rule/interval mixture with guessing allows.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values
    n = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(axis=1)
    par = np.where(np.isnan(ex), np.nan, np.mod(ex, 2))
    s = np.nansum(par, axis=1)
    all_odd = (s == n)
    all_even = (s == 0)
    tp = df["target"].astype(int).values % 2
    mask = (n >= 2) & ((all_odd & (tp == 0)) | (all_even & (tp == 1)))
    if mask.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].values[mask].mean())

results.name: single_example_proximity_gradient
results.description: For single-example sets, yes-rate on non-example targets within 10 of the example minus yes-rate on targets more than 30 away; observed > model means people generalize from one example by numeric magnitude similarity more than the model's rule/interval posterior predicts, observed < model means magnitude matters less than predicted.
results.code:
# name: single_example_proximity_gradient
# description: For single-example sets, yes-rate on non-example targets within 10 of the example minus yes-rate on targets more than 30 away; observed > model means people generalize from one example by numeric magnitude similarity more than the model's rule/interval posterior predicts, observed < model means magnitude matters less than predicted.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    single = ~s.str.contains(",").values
    x = pd.to_numeric(s.where(single, "nan"), errors="coerce").values
    tgt = df["target"].astype(float).values
    d = np.abs(tgt - x)
    near = single & (d > 0) & (d <= 10)
    far = single & (d > 30)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    if near.sum() == 0 or far.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[near].mean() - r[far].mean())

results.name: near_rule_outlier_rule_yes
results.description: For 3-4-example sets where exactly all-but-one examples share a last digit or divisibility by 3..10 (and not all do), yes-rate on non-example targets that fit that shared rule and lie outside the range of the rule-fitting examples; observed > model means people keep a near-fitting rule despite an exception more than the model's inferred stray-example tolerance predicts, observed < model means they abandon it more readily.
results.code:
# name: near_rule_outlier_rule_yes
# description: For 3-4-example sets where exactly all-but-one examples share a last digit or divisibility by 3..10 (and not all do), yes-rate on non-example targets that fit that shared rule and lie outside the range of the rule-fitting examples; observed > model means people keep a near-fitting rule despite an exception more than the model's inferred stray-example tolerance predicts, observed < model means they abandon it more readily.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values
    n = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(axis=1)
    tgt = df["target"].astype(float).values
    valid_ex = ~np.isnan(ex)
    exf = np.where(valid_ex, ex, 0.0)
    is_ex = ((exf == tgt[:, None]) & valid_ex).any(axis=1)
    hit = np.zeros(len(df), dtype=bool)
    tests = [("mod10", d) for d in range(10)] + [("div", k) for k in range(3, 11)]
    for kind, v in tests:
        if kind == "mod10":
            fit = (np.mod(exf, 10) == v) & valid_ex
            tfit = np.mod(tgt, 10) == v
        else:
            fit = (np.mod(exf, v) == 0) & valid_ex
            tfit = np.mod(tgt, v) == 0
        cnt = fit.sum(axis=1)
        cond = (n >= 3) & (cnt == n - 1)
        lo = np.where(fit, exf, np.inf).min(axis=1)
        hi = np.where(fit, exf, -np.inf).max(axis=1)
        outside = (tgt < lo) | (tgt > hi)
        hit |= cond & tfit & outside & (~is_ex)
    if hit.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].values[hit].mean())

results.name: recency_nearest_last_minus_first
results.description: Among non-example targets of 2+-example sets, yes-rate when the target's nearest example is the last-shown one minus yes-rate when it is the first-shown one; observed > model means a recency effect (generalization anchored on the most recent example) that the order-invariant model cannot produce, observed < model means a primacy effect.
results.code:
# name: recency_nearest_last_minus_first
# description: Among non-example targets of 2+-example sets, yes-rate when the target's nearest example is the last-shown one minus yes-rate when it is the first-shown one; observed > model means a recency effect (generalization anchored on the most recent example) that the order-invariant model cannot produce, observed < model means a primacy effect.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values
    n = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(axis=1)
    tgt = df["target"].astype(float).values
    d = np.abs(ex - tgt[:, None])
    d = np.where(np.isnan(d), np.inf, d)
    is_ex = (d == 0).any(axis=1)
    nearest = np.argmin(d, axis=1)
    dmin = d.min(axis=1)
    last_idx = n - 1
    d_last = d[np.arange(len(d)), last_idx]
    d_first = d[:, 0]
    valid = (n >= 2) & (~is_ex)
    near_last = valid & (d_last == dmin) & (d_first > dmin)
    near_first = valid & (d_first == dmin) & (d_last > dmin)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    if near_last.sum() == 0 or near_first.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[near_last].mean() - r[near_first].mean())

results.name: outside_range_near_minus_far
results.description: Among non-example targets lying outside the [min, max] range of a 2+-example set, yes-rate for targets within 10 of the range minus yes-rate for targets more than 25 beyond it; observed > model means people's generalization falls off with distance outside the examples more steeply than the model's interval/rule mixture predicts, observed < model means a flatter falloff.
results.code:
# name: outside_range_near_minus_far
# description: Among non-example targets lying outside the [min, max] range of a 2+-example set, yes-rate for targets within 10 of the range minus yes-rate for targets more than 25 beyond it; observed > model means people's generalization falls off with distance outside the examples more steeply than the model's interval/rule mixture predicts, observed < model means a flatter falloff.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values
    n = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1)
    hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    tgt = df["target"].astype(float).values
    dist = np.maximum(lo - tgt, tgt - hi)
    valid = (n >= 2) & (dist > 0)
    near = valid & (dist <= 10)
    far = valid & (dist > 25)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    if near.sum() == 0 or far.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[near].mean() - r[far].mean())

results.name: example_target_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate on trials whose target is one of the shown examples; observed > model means people endorse already-shown examples more reliably than the model (whose guessing dilutes these near-certain items) predicts, observed < model means they endorse them less.
